utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. Mr. McCloskey is here for the Prosecution today. And from amongst the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Ms. Nikolic. Good morning to you, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are going to continue with Mr. Haynes' examination-in-chief and then we will see what happens after that. Mr. Haynes, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday evening, Mr. Jevdjevic, we were talking about the two communication systems that you set up at the IKM at Pribicevac, the encrypted system which you used to communicate with the units on the ground and the radio relay system which you used to communicate with corps command. In relation to the radio relay system, was that also capable of communicating with individual brigade commands?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How could that be facilitated?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio relay communications could not be integrated into -- with the units that participated in Krivaja 95 operation, if I understood your question correctly; but it could be used to establish contacts with the original commands of those units in the garrisons of Bratunac, Vlasenica, Zvornik, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you didn't understand my question, but you anticipated my next question so you probably saved us a bit of time. So if a commander on the ground, such as Commander Pandurevic, wanted to get in touch with his brigade command, what were his options?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only option was to come to the forward command post at Pribicevac, or later on at the forward command around Zepa, personally, and to use the phone, the communications equipment there, to communicate with his original command in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to show you a couple of documents very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we look at P377 at page 96, both in the English and the B/C/S. In fact, that may be not the best document to look at. Can we look at P378, please, page 83.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is the Zvornik Brigade duty officer's diary for the 5th of July, and if you look at the very top entry, it appears to reflect a request from Commander Pandurevic to his brigade command for them to send him some ammunition for a tank. Now, on the 5th of July, in terms of the communication system, what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 5th of July in the early afternoon, I came to the forward command post at Pribicevac and some ten minutes later I was able to establish communications with the superior command, i.e., the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica. And I was able to establish radio communications with the subordinate units that took part in Operation Krivaja 95 which, by that time, had already been in their holding areas around the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall any conversation with Commander Pandurevic about a need for tank ammunition on the 5th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I established contact with all the units just to check whether the communication lines were good, whether we could all hear each other, and to check whether anyone had any needs, because that was the first time that we all got together at that part of the front line, and since I was the only person able to communicate with the corps command in terms of providing logistics support, things like that. I don't recall specifically any conversations, but if this is the telegram as noted down by the operations officer at -- by the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade at 1700 hours, by that time communications were already set up. And I absolutely allow that it is possible that this either went through me -- in other words, that I was told by Commander Pandurevic to relay this message to the duty operations officer in the Zvornik Brigade because it says here, "Sent a message." This means that this message was relayed through somebody, asking that 50 shells be sent to him to the new forward command post, because this was the practice, the usual practice, how those messages that had to do with logistics were relayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we just have another look at a further page in the duty officer's logbook this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: P377, page 101, both in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you see the entry at 1110 concerning an apparent call from Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic and a request to hand something over to the faculty. During the period that the communications centre was active at Pribicevac, do you ever recall Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic coming to the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this about the 7th of July, because I can't see the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it is the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am almost completely certain that on the 7th of July the front line was quiet because it was a rainy day, and then dense fog descended so that on the seventh day, the units of the Drina Corps at that part of the front line did not engage in combat at all, and they were strengthening their combat disposition, and perhaps some corrective decisions were made. And the Zvornik Brigade carried out an attack from the Zeleni Jadar-Tucak-Javor base, in the area of the road leading to Srebrenica. This Javor hill is about a kilometre and a half or two from the forward command post Pribicevac, and I absolutely allow that it is possible that on that day, when the combat disposition was being strengthened and when no combat went on, that Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic was able to travel the kilometre and a half to the forward command post to relay this message to the command of his brigade. It was probably some materiel -- or rather some materials to be handed over to the faculty. I assume that it was the faculty in Zvornik because at that time he was an assistant lecturer or something like that at that faculty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I am going to leave the communications system now and very, very briefly run through some of the details of the combat operations of Krivaja 95 insofar as you can recall them. You told us that combat commenced on the 6th of July. Was any or much progress made by the forces of the Drina Corps on the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, our forces carried out reconnaissance in force in order to establish where points of resistance was located, and apart from an area between the two sets of trenches that were taken, there were no major developments in terms of combat situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. From the forward command post at Pribicevac, could you see the two features Biljak and Tri Sise?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were they taken in combat operations on the 8th and/or 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in general terms, were you aware of the size of the force that had been assembled to carry out Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And about how large was it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this two days ago. It was my assessment that the overall strength of the maneuver units that participated in Krivaja 95, that were actually involved in the attack, did not exceed 1.000 troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I've asked you a question you were asked before, but did you have also information as to the size of the defending force in and around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all the data that we had at our disposal and that we had been receiving for years, in the Srebrenica enclave there were between 10 and 15.000 men of military age, and we thought that at least 10 to 12.000 were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in terms of the surrounding terrain, was Srebrenica an easy or difficult town to defend?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrain itself around Srebrenica, it's a hilly, mountainous ground, impassable because of the gorges, canyons, and there are dominant heights; and in geographical terms, this kind of terrain is highly favourable for mounting a defence. And it is very difficult to attack in such terrain and to take the heights, to cross the gorges and canyons and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Given everything you've told us, was it your opinion that the forces assembled to carry out Krivaja 95 were designed to take the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the equivalent of the forces, if you compare it with the forces defending the area, in military terms, even if you are the most optimistic person you could not even imagine that such a number of troops could inflict a defeat on 12.000 troops. Because according to our military doctrine, the attacking side has to have three times as many soldiers and as much support for the attack to succeed, given this kind of terrain. I did say something to that effect about two days ago. In 1993, based on my personal knowledge, we had much more respectable forces in the area and yet we came to a stop at this position, Pribicevac and Kvarac. And I remember that at the time our crack unit, the Guards Brigade, in two hours of combat at trig point 1313 Kvarac, suffered 30 casualties. 30 people were rendered hors de combat because they were either killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you were talking about a feature to the south of Srebrenica called Zivkovo Brdo. Can you just confirm for me - I know you've probably said this before - on what date that feature was taken by the forces of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps forces took that elevation on the 9th of July, and this was the first major success of our forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you just confirm for me under whose command the unit was which took Zivkovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those units were under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: After Zivkovo Brdo had been taken, what did the units commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic do?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that were under the command of Vinko Pandurevic, in the night or, rather, in the early evening of the 9th, secured the positions at Zivkovo Brdo that were reached so that the units of the Skelani Battalion could join in in the taking and holding those positions. Those were the units that were holding the positions around Srebrenica, enabling his units to pull out to an area about a kilometre or a kilometre -- or two kilometres into the rear, in order to get some rest and prepare for further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I wonder now if we could have another look at a document you've seen before. It's P107, and we want to look at point 5 please. I think it's on page 3 of both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you see under point 5 that the task of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade is to smash the enemy along the axis of advance and, more immediately, to capture the trig point 644 Zivkovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I am not sure whether you remember the trig points, but is that the hill, the feature you are talking about, that's mentioned in that document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact trig point, but it's definitely Zivkovo Brdo. That's the trig point that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in terms of sound military practice, does it surprise you that having achieved its task, the unit commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic withdrew from Zivkovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we had only the smaller equivalent of the forces carrying out the attacks, and it is quite possible that a smaller element, in order to secure the lines that were reached, that this battle group from the Zvornik Brigade that was carrying out an attack on this axis may have left a smaller element in that area to secure the front line. I think those were two or three resistance points armed with Pragas, and to my knowledge, the main body of force actually went back to spend the night there, to sleep, get some sleep in order to be fresh and to be able to carry out further tasks, any task that may be ordered by the commander of the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We see at the end of that particular paragraph the phrase, "Be ready to continue the attack." Have you seen many operational documents in your time as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in relative terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the phrase, "Be ready to continue the attack," is that unusual or is that a common phrase that's used in such documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a quite usual expression, it's a common phrase. One finds it in all the forms in which such orders are written. It's used on all occasions regardless of whether there will be a real need for any continuation of the activities or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Judge Kwon, did you mean the next page in English or in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we are seeing page 4, its okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you've already told us this, but what happened on the early morning of the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, in the early morning between 4.00 and 5.00, at the forward command post in Pribicevac the alarm was raised. We were all awake and on our feet because there was fierce fire at the Zivkovo Brdo trig point, and we received information from the radio communications that the enemy forces from the Srebrenica enclave had launched a fierce counter-attack. And that in a very brief period of time, they had pushed back our units which had taken Zivkovo Brdo the previous day. According to the communications we listened to, our forces were withdrawing in a disorganised manner. Some of our men were killed and some of our equipment was captured. But two hours after the counter-attack was launched, our units managed to consolidate and stop any further enemy advance. They managed to regroup for a counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, where was Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic was at his forward command post, and I remember that at around 9.00 on the 10th of June --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: July, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when General Mladic arrived at the forward command post, I remember the conversation between Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic and Ratko Mladic concerning the situation I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you summarise that conversation for us to the best of your ability now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As all of us at the forward command post were rather concerned because the previous day we had been encouraged by the initial success and then the military situation was reversed, I recall that General Mladic contacted Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic who, at that point, had managed to consolidate his battle disposition. And I remember that Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic told him how dissatisfied he was with the response of the neighbouring units which were attacking to his left and to his right. I assume he was referring to their passivity in dealing with this military situation. And, in my view, he said in a very brilliant and self-assured manner to General Mladic that he would recapture Zivkovo Brdo by 11.00. I thought this was unrealistic. I thought it was very bold of him to say that, but a few hours later it really happened that way on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the village of Pusmulici?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the name is Pusmulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the village of Pusmulic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where is that in relation to the feature Zivkovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the map before me now, but viewed from the direction of the attack it was on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday, when answering questions to Mr. Petrusic, that on the 10th of July General Mladic was urging all the commanders towards Srebrenica. Did you understand him to be urging the commanders, on the 10th of July, actually to enter the town or just to get closer to it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, I understood him to be ordering the commanders to advance towards the town, to approach the town, because their position on the battlefield was still so far away from Srebrenica that it was not realistic to expect him to order them to enter Srebrenica at that time. He was simply hurrying them up, trying to get them to pierce through to the features that were set as the next goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when, to your recollection, did any order come to actually enter the town itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this order was issued only on the 11th when our units or, rather, when we passed through the town, but on the 11th, when I passed through the town, I did not see our units there. But quite literally, I had the impression that on the 11th the town was no longer being defended, and that the 28th Division of Bosnia and Herzegovina had ceased to exist and that they had left the area, grouping mostly on the northwest -- in the northwest part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the 11th of July, did you have occasion to meet Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In what circumstances did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, the combat situation developed in such a way that we received information from the battlefield that the enemy was not putting up any significant resistance anywhere. And some of our units, which were still very far away, which had lagged behind, had to be transported along the road to get as close to the front line as possible. General Krstic, because I was familiar with that part of the terrain, sent me to the area of Alibegovac where I was supposed to take a company from the 2nd Romanija Brigade, which would find it very difficult to advance over that impassable terrain over such a distance, to take them by way of Jasenova and Zeleni Jadar to the area between Rajna and Bojna and to get them to join in the combat activities in that area because they were very late. When I had done that, in the area between the village of Rajna and Bojna, I met Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic with his communications man, who was in an improvised shelter. We spoke. I told him about this unit, which was now supposed to be his left-hand neighbour, and at that point in time the NATO planes flew over. And I remember that a bomb was dropped very close to where we were on the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road, and the windscreen of the jeep of the commander of the maneuver unit, Captain Jolovic, shattered. On that day, the 11th, I met Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I just want to ask you a few general questions about the combat operations between the 6th and the 11th of July. Did you come to learn, through communications on the ground, of the proximity of 28th Division positions to UN observation posts?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the attack of our forces on the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road, near those three nameless elevations which we called the three tits, there was a trig point called Biljeg, and on that trig point there was a UN observation post. On the communications, I listened to the subordinate commanders communicating with General Krstic about the problem of that elevation called Biljeg because UNPROFOR was stationed there. General Krstic did not find it in his interest to have the complications -- to have complications regarding the UNPROFOR situation, so he ordered his commanders to go around them, to bypass them by every possible means, both with infantry and everything else. But the commanders complained that the formations of the 28th Division, which were defending themselves in that area, had infiltrated into the improvised shelters of UNPROFOR and were firing from there on our units. And this complicated the combat situation significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you've already told us about what General Krstic's orders were in relation to UNPROFOR, so I won't ask you that again. What about targets within the town of Srebrenica itself? Did you hear anything suggesting that artillery fire was being directed at the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The support we had for the Srebrenica operation was a unit which was in the communications plan, and that was the Mixed Artillery Regiment, and I remember that Colonel Borovina was the commander of that regiment. And that for this operation in this part of the war theater, we had only two artillery pieces, I think they were howitzers, 150-millimetre howitzers, and I know that the commanders of the subordinate units --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 105 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- asked for support on targets along the line they were attacking simply so that the artillery could soften the points of resistance. And there was no need for them to ask for any shelling of any goals in the depth of the territory, and here I'm referring to the town of Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We mentioned briefly the village of Pusmulic. Did it become apparent to you, through the communications centre, that that was an area, at some stage, that was being used as a defensive position by the forces of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember those particular details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one last thing. Presumably you saw quite a number of the forces assembled to conduct Operation Krivaja 95. Did you ever see any VRS forces that were equipped with dogs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to move on now to the meeting in Bratunac on the 11th of July. Do you have any recollection now of who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic chaired the meeting. On his left- and right-hand side were General Zivanovic and General Krstic. I remember, as I've already stated, I am not sure how many commanders were absent, maybe one or two, but as I said almost all of the commanders participating in the Krivaja 95 operation were there. I remember that Lieutenant-Colonel Furtula was there also, he was the commander of the Visegrad Brigade which had not participated in the operation. And of course I remember very well that Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who spoke at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly General Mladic who spoke at that meeting. He set out briefly a description of the newly arisen situation. He was satisfied with the military success that had been achieved, and after this analysis by him, he said that on the following day all the units that had participated in the attack on Srebrenica -- or, rather, in the Operation Krivaja 95, should regroup and immediately march and begin an attack on Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic also speak?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic did speak, and I remember very well what he said to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You may have told us this in summary before, but to the best of your recollection, can you tell us what he said?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic described a situation in which we did not have precise information as to where the 28th Division was. In his opinion, this division was still a potential problem because the situation was very unclear. If they wanted to breakthrough in the direction of Tuzla, this could be a significant problem both for the forces around Srebrenica and for the depth of our territory in the direction of Tuzla. He proposed to General Mladic that it would be a very good idea if this situation was cleared up in military terms, the military situation in Srebrenica, so that later on we could carry out his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was Mladic's response?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic listened to this proposal and said right away, Regardless of all that, tomorrow everyone has to go towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it unusual for what I'll call a junior officer to stand up to General Mladic in that way?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic was a commander who was very authoritarian, and it was unusual for us, for someone who was junior both to General Krstic, General Zivanovic, and all the other colonels, to put forward such an obvious and rational proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, did this meeting take place on the eve of a particular religious festival?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held on the 11th of July, and on the 12th of July, according to the Christian calendar, it was St. Peter's Day. Is that the day you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's not for me to answer your questions, but you've answered mine. And is there a particular tradition as to what one eats on the eve of St. Peter's Day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Christian calendar, St. Peter's Day is the end of a major fast. And on the 11th of July, the last day of the fast, Christian believers eat food which is suitable for a fast day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was there a meal prior to the meeting on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any meal before the meeting, but after the end of the meeting, when I received an order from General Mladic and when we rose and everyone was going to go about his own business, suddenly the door of this larger office opened and someone called Zvonko Bajagic entered, he was a man from Vlasenica, a householder, working in the logistics of the Drina Corps, and he carrying a huge oval platter with a huge fish on it. I remembered that because I found it unusual, in military terms, but I saw that as connected with the fast day. After that I immediately left the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And is there any doubt in your mind that the meeting you've told us about occurred on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never doubted that. I am absolutely sure it was on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to clear up a few details, you were, as you told us, dispatched Krivace by General Mladic on the 11th of July. Did you go directly there or did you stop somewhere else first?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, at around 2400 hours, I arrived in the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, which was on the road towards Han Pijesak and Krivace. I dropped in to see the duty operations officer to evaluate the situation. I needed to repair a vehicle, the vehicle we used to transport the mobile communications centre. I knew that I was far more mobile than the units in Srebrenica were and that I would get to the Zepa area before them. That's why I decided to give my men a rest, to replenish our equipment, our generators, and then following the development of the situation, to go on to Zepa on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you in fact do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I did. And on the following day in the morning, I was already at the forward command post at Krivace, between Han Pijesak and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you establish from Krivace communications with corps command in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived there on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you receive communications from corps command from that moment onwards?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you understand the forces which had conducted Operation Krivaja 95 to be engaged in on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it very unusual in view of the fact that on the 11th of July, in the evening, General Mladic had ordered everyone to move towards Zepa on the following day. I found it unusual that the units which had participated in Krivaja 95 were not arriving in Zepa already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When in fact did they arrive in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived in the holding areas around Zepa in the night between the 13th and the 14th of July, for the most part. In the meantime, I learned that in this area around Vijogora [phoen], between Milici, Podravanje, and Suceska, were carrying out a search operation of the terrain, resting their personnel, and that they had a line-up and a brief meeting with General Mladic. And then after that, in marching columns, they took various axes because they were afraid of the air-strikes. And under cover of the night, they regrouped for the waiting operations with the attack operations in Operation Stupcanica 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to look at a document for us now, please. You've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's P114.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You recognise this document, Mr. Jevdjevic, I imagine?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not receive this document myself but I had an opportunity to look at it in the proofing for my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who would have written this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was signed, I think, by General Krstic, and that's what it probably says on the last page of this document. And it was probably on his orders and under his instructions that this document was drafted by Colonel Vicic, who was at General Krstic's side at all times in the course of both Operation Krivaja 95 and Stupcanica 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Vicic's position changed, as we understand it, sometime around about this period. What was his position at the beginning of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise about it. I think that he was in the operations organ. But for the purpose of those two operations, he had full trust of General Krstic because he was a professional officer, he had undergone military training, and he was familiar with all the jobs, all tasks, within his purview, and he was there at his side at all times throughout those two operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after General Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps, what role did Colonel Vicic then have?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he became the chief of the operations department in the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. And did he have any specific role in Krivaja 95 or in Stupcanica 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was simply in the service of General Krstic, and all the information from the front lines came to him. He drafted the reports and whatever General Krstic ordered him to do. Any concepts that he may have had, he turned them into written documents and he took care of all the correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we'll leave that there. The forward command post at Krivace, what was the visual capability there over the combat area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krivace is a dominant height. It gives a clear line of vision of all the terrain, the enclave of Zepa, and even further from the enclave itself. It's a hilly, mountainous terrain which is densely wooded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you aware, not just, as it were, through the communications system, but visually, of the arrival of the units commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic in the area around Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In front of us in the valley itself there is a large field. This is where the villages of Podzeplje and Plane are located. There is a large meadow where those two fields are, a plain of sorts, and I saw it myself when the Zvornik Brigade units came. They were quite striking because they had two -- they had vehicles that were used for combat purposes, because they had machine-guns mounted on them. I saw them station themselves in the Podzeplje village, in the village of Podzeplje, and that's where they set up their forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On what date was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 14th, in the morning of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what combat activity, if any, did those units conduct on the day of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, an approach march was carried out from the deployment line to the front end of the enemy defence lines. This area was quite remote because the village of Podzeplje, which was under our control, and the Brlog mountain where we assumed that the front defence positions were -- Brloska mountain, Planina, where we assumed that the Zepa Brigade defence positions at the front end were located, they are quite far away. So it was only at the early evening that our forces were able to come close to the Zepa Brigade units. And throughout the 14th, this was the activity that was carried out, and there were no major operations or actions apart from maybe some sporadic actions and reconnaissance in force that was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have talked previously about Major Dragan Obrenovic. Is he somebody you had known all your life?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We are quite literally from the same village. We were born in the same year and we completed all our schools together in the same year. We were in the same class all the up -- down to military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you hear from him at any time during the 14th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a telephone conversation on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you help us as to about what time that telephone conversation was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very well that it was on the 14th. I don't know the exact time, but I do know what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, just approximately, was it in the morning, afternoon, or evening?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is logical to assume that it was not in the morning, not in the evening, but in the middle of the day or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this might seem an odd question, why do you think he called you in particular?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Obrenovic, that was his rank at the time, called me and he was very much concerned. He told me that the military situation in the Zvornik area was very unfavorable because he had received information about a huge column of the 28th Division that was carrying out a breakthrough out of the encirclement, going through the defences of his units, that his reconnaissance units had already been in close contact with those units, with the column, and that he did not have enough men to deploy, to carry out those combat missions. And I simply had a feeling that he had already discussed this with somebody from the corps command. Then he told me, I have a feeling that the guys from the superior command do not have any understanding from my position that they have -- that they fail to understand the magnitude of the problem I am facing. You know that I am not afraid, that's what he told me, and that I am not a coward, but this is a huge problem. And I would like to ask you, therefore, to present this situation to General Krstic in some way so that he could make his decision and to give him back the battle group that was under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic at the Zepa front line in order to assist him in dealing with this problem. At the forward command post, some ten metres away from me, General Krstic was there, and it was quite unusual to me that Major Obrenovic was telling me about this problem. But the reason why he did that was because he thought that the superior officers did not take the situation seriously enough, and he was hoping, since I was there closer to General Krstic and that I knew him, and I knew Obrenovic very well, that I would be able to paint a more vivid picture of the problem to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jevdjevic. And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I relayed all that to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how did General Krstic respond?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that time General Krstic knew, from a military standpoint, that the problems that Major Obrenovic was facing were quite real. But he, himself, faced another problem. If, in order to solve those problems he were to send Colonel Pandurevic and his unit back to that area, then the whole concept of the attack - in other words Stupcanica 95 - would be jeopardized. So he was in two minds for a long time how to juggle those two problems, how to deal with those two problems at the opposite ends of the corps area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So on the afternoon of the 14th of July, what decision did he take?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, he was still assessing the situation, that was my opinion, and I don't recall any specific decisions that he made relating to this plea on the part of Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, did he order Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic to go back to Zvornik on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he even call Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic to the forward command post to discuss the matter with him on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic was quite far away, in the direction of the Brloska mountains, carrying out the reconnaissance in force, and that was the first time that his unit was actually deployed in Stupcanica 95, in that operation. So that on that day General Krstic, regarding the problems in Zvornik, did not have any contacts with Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now what time on the 14th of July did General Krstic leave the forward command post for the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, after receiving reports about the situation at the front line and once he was sure that the situation was okay, General Krstic would go to a neighbouring village to see his wife's parents and to spend the night there, because at that time he had big problems with the prosthetic leg that he had fitted after he lost his leg in a shell explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but I don't think you did answer the question, which is: About what time was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He always left in the evening around 9.00 or 10.00. That's when he would leave the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if we could now put into e-court, please, a succession of documents. Firstly, P169.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, that's a report to the Drina Corps command. It's dated the 14th of July and timed at 2230 hours. Did that come through to the forward command post at Krivace on the evening of the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This report designated as "Very urgent, attention Krstic," arrived at 2230. And it was received by Oliver Sekulic, my cryptographer at the forward command post. He signed it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did General Krstic see that before he retired for the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this document came after he left the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we look at another one, please, P327.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is an interim combat report from the Zvornik Brigade to the Drina Corps, dated the 15th of July, in the very small hours of the morning at 10 past 1.00. Did that come through to the forward command post at Krivace?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say that. I can't really see it here, but I assume that since this information was meant for General Krstic, that one of his assistants or the duty operations officer at the corps command in Vlasenica forwarded that to the forward command post at Krivace because at that time it was a very significant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the following morning, on the 15th of July, at what time did General Krstic arrive at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic would arrive at the forward command post in the morning at around 7.00 a.m., sometimes earlier, sometimes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we now look at, please, P163.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A report of the 4th Radio Reconnaissance Platoon describing the situation towards Zvornik, addressed to the commander of the Drina Corps. Did that arrive at the forward command post on the morning of the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when General Krstic arrived for duty on the morning of the 15th of July, was he given three documents to look at concerning the situation in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, it's not, because the answer can be either yes or no. A leading question is one which suggests the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is. A specific number of documents is something coming directly from the mind of the lawyer. I mean, it's so easy to get around that. Why do -- why is he -- why does it have to be three?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We seem to be in disagreement here, but basically --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the beginning I thought it wasn't leading. But I see that you specifically refer to three documents, so that makes it leading according to me, but anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Fine. Fine, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was General Krstic provided with information about the situation in Zvornik when he arrived for duty on the morning of the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every morning when he came to the forward command post, General Krstic always familiarised himself with the situation at the front line, and he would be shown all the telegrams that had arrived in his absence to the forward command post so that he had an opportunity to read all the telegrams and to familiarise himself with the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jevdjevic. But on that particular morning, was his attention directed to the situation in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The focus of his activity and the reading of the documents was precisely on the situation that the Zvornik Brigade command encountered in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to satisfy everybody's curiosity, was he given one, two, three, four, five or more documents?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gave him all the documents, including the three documents that we are talking about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was very concerned. And he made a decision at that time, and he ordered me to use the radio equipment to invite Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, the commander of that battle group, to come to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came to the forward command post in his vehicle and with an escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long after General Krstic had reviewed the material did he do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he arrived maybe 20 minutes or half an hour later in the motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did any discussion follow or did General Krstic just issue him with an order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic briefed him about the new developments in the Zvornik area, briefly, about the documents that he had received that dealt with those problems, and ordered him -- in fact, told him that the only way to deal with it was to take the whole unit involved in Operation Stupcanica in Zepa and to immediately return to the Zvornik area to solve the problem. And I know that after that conversation, Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic wanted to acquaint himself with the situation in Zvornik himself, and he told me to set up a communications line with the Zvornik Brigade command, and he also used the other communications equipment to call all of his commanders who were still at the Zepa front line and issued some preliminary orders to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, about what time of the morning was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at around 8.30 or thereabouts, that was when he talked to his brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jevdjevic. I am nearly at an end but we are due a break, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when you say nearly, how near? Is it a matter of five minutes, in other words? Because if it's five minutes, we can go a further five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It might be ten because there are some documents involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's have the break. Thank you. 25 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, good morning. Good morning, everyone. This is just a short point. As we are getting to cross-examination -- could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are now in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Going back to where I left you just before we had a break, we were at the forward command post at Krivace, and you were describing how Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic was making contact with his brigade back in Zvornik. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to act as a sort of aide-memoire for you, I want to show you a few documents to see if they remind you of that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we'll start with P117 A in English. P1171 B in B/C/S. It's 1171. I -- I've got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, we are going to test the system straight away. You will know from your previous experience here at the Tribunal that certain communications on the open line were allegedly intercepted by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You've heard of that, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this is an example of that, and you should look at the bottom of that page, and this is said to be at 8.34 on the morning of the 15th of July. Do you have any recollection that you were a participant in a conversation where you were told that Semso Muminovic was asking to speak to Vinko Pandurevic and leaving a telephone number?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left the frequency they should talk on, and most probably, as I remember the event, this commander Semso Muminovic, who was on the Tuzla side in that area of responsibility between the Zvornik Brigade and the Tuzla Corps, he had probably already had some communications with Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic. And I allow for the possibility that someone talked to me and conveyed this message to me, asking me to try to find Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic and tell him that this Semso Muminovic was asking to speak to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now can we go to P1173. A in the English and B in Serbian. Yes. I'm sorry. Can we have D in the B/C/S, please, because it gives us the date, which B doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we can take this quite shortly. You've seen this document before, haven't you? This is another transcript of an intercept --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And does it accord with your recollection of one of the calls which Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic made from the forward command post on the morning of the 15th of July -- 14th -- 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I established communications for him with the command of the brigade in Zvornik and that he didn't find Major Obrenovic there at the time, his Chief of Staff. And I know that he spoke with some officers from his command, and that they discussed the combat situation. But I don't know, or I didn't know at the time, precisely with what officers he spoke; whereas, here I can see that they were Milosevic and Mijatovic. I knew them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to complete the picture, can we have P1174. A in the English and B in the B/C/S. I think it's already up in the B/C/S, so I'll proceed with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall one call made by Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic or more than one call from the forward command post that morning?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What forward command post are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Krivace.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning when General Krstic conveyed to Vinko what the situation was in the area of his brigade in Zvornik and ordered him to come back with the unit from Zepa in order to deal with the military part of that situation, Vinko asked for additional information and he asked to contact his command in Zvornik personally. He spoke to some officers from the command of his brigade about these problems. That's all I know from my personal knowledge at the time because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to summarise events at the forward command post on the morning of the 15th of July. Did you see any document that came through on the teleprinter that made any reference to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did any of the discussion between General Krstic and Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic concern prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And from what you could hear of what Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic was saying to Milosevic or Mijatovic or Jokic, who we can see that he spoke to in one of these conversations, did any of those conversations concern prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just to complete the picture. Did Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic withdraw his units from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that a straightforward process or did it take a little time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, logically, it took some time for that because it wasn't easy to pull out a unit which was in contact with the enemy, in combat in impassable terrain on a mountain. And then the commander, General Krstic, had to introduce another unit into this gap, this breach gap, so that this hand-over of positions, which the Zvornik Brigade had taken up to that morning, required some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to look briefly at another intercept, if we can. It's P1176. A in the English and B in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you understand the code names Palma and Zlatar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document is under seal so be careful what use you make of it, and it's not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, do you understand that the duty officer at Palma was the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the duty officer in the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And Zlatar was the code name for the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the code name for the Drina Corps in that period of time, and this conversation probably refers to the duty officer in the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's recorded as being a conversation taking place on channel three, what does that tell you about where it originated from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous conversations had the frequency entered here that corresponds to the frequency range of the RRU1 equipment. We did not have cryptographic protection on that equipment, and I assume this was between the Krivace forward command post and Velika Zepa [as interpreted] because that was the sort of equipment we used on that channel. This is probably RRU800, the radio relay equipment active from Vlasenica to the stationery switchboard of Veliki Zep, and with that equipment we communicated with the brigade commands in Zvornik, Sekovici, and Rogatica, and I assumed that this can only refer to that equipment. It would be even clearer to me if whoever drew up this document had also entered the frequency of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you've seen this intercept before. What does it appear to you to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my interpretation, as I understand this conversation, in view of the fact that in the command of the Zvornik Brigade, the situation regarding the problems they had because the 28th Division was passing through their area of responsibility, before a written telegram was sent, someone wanted to encourage them and comfort them and tell them that their special formation was on the way back from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. It's in quite cloudy language. Would that be normal to -- in conveying such a message over an open line?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand this, probably the duty officer at Zlatar wanted to conceal this information from anyone listening in, so he told the duty officer at Palma, that is in Zvornik, something that the other one didn't understand, which is why he cursed. He said, "Our men -- with our lot with the boss," and this corresponds to the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now look at 7D686.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The time on this order is 1041, and can you tell us what this order is or this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the command of the Drina Corps in which on the 15th of July, while this document was being dictated and typed out and encrypted, a certain amount of time elapsed. And the person who encrypted it handed it over in the Zvornik Brigade at 1041. The document itself is to inform the command of the Zvornik Brigade in writing that the combat composition which had been engaged at Zepa was returning to its original area of responsibility, and it explains why that is, in order to prevent the consequences of a possible attack on Zvornik and the joining up of Muslim formations from Srebrenica and Tuzla and that all measures should be taken to block and, if possible, rout and capture the Muslim formations before the arrival of this unit and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so that we are clear, could Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic have returned to Zvornik without an order from General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. You've already told us, but the communication plan for Stupcanica 95, did that in any way differ than that which had been in operation for Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was the same communications plan. It was identical. The only thing we changed was the location of the forward command post, so we just had to alter the azimuth of the antenna for the RRU equipment at the Veliki Zep node. And this other plan included as reserve participants the Rogatica and Visegrad Brigades which had not taken part in the Krivaja Operation but they did take part in the Stupcanica operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so did you still retain as part of the network the Zvornik Brigade with its appropriate code name?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was identical. The same plan remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you answered some questions to Mr. Petrusic about the combat and the evacuation of Zepa. Did you, during any of that period, have any communications over that network with any unit of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am going to show you just two more documents and then we are done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at P1353. And that's A in the English and B in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is another transcript of a conversation said to be between Major Jevdzevic, would that be you, and somebody called Vinko. Would that be Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume so because at that time I did not know of any other Vinko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it appears to concern the combat situation in Zepa and whether Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic is going to be required to come back there. Do you recall having such a conversation on or about the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that conversation roughly, in general terms, but I wasn't sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's just been pointed out to me that, in fact, on the B/C/S the conversation begins at the very bottom of the page, and perhaps the next page of that document is what the witness should have to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you see that the person called Vinko asks you: "Have you gone over to the Zepa side?" And you said: "Well, I sort of have." "Is the work going all right?" "It is going all right." "Are they going to ask me to go there?" "Probably not." And you apparently said: "We will see today. Last night a big convoy went ..." and so on. And "Where is their army?" Are you following that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you see, after the 15th of July, Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic at the theater at Zepa at all?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just lastly I want to you to look at a different -- well, another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's P3893.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this goes back to some questions I asked you yesterday. Can you see the name bottom of that document, Jovicic Nedo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This document hasn't been translated, but can you tell us what it appears to be, what it appears to say?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the heading it is handwritten, "The command of the Drina Corps, Pribicevac forward command post." The date is the 11th of July. It is addressed to the command of the special police brigade. The subject is, "Combat documents delivered herewith." And it says here: "We hereby deliver to you the coded map Grmec, the code book Krivaja 95, the work plan Krivaja 95, and call signs, strictly confidential, 04/156-3."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we go to page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We've seen that before as P3753, that's the communication plan. Did you recognise the writing on the handwritten document on page 1 of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with this letter? Did you write it or ask for it to be written?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you know it had been done?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jevdjevic. Although we know each other, let me introduce myself for the record. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and in this case I defend Vujadin Popovic. My question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need the lectern?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The lectern? No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't used it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My questions, Mr. Jevdjevic, will be limited to the organisation and the functioning of the communications in this period that we are all interested in and at the time when you were the commander of the 5th Battalion, the Communications Battalion in the Drina Corps. We have spoken about this at length here and we have an expert report drafted by Mr. Djuro Rodic where he states, inter alia, that in addition to all the documents that we provided him, he consulted you when he was drafting that document. It is 1D321 tendered by us. It's at page 6 in the English version; at page 5 of the B/C/S version. That's at paragraph 221. Now, I would like to ask you if you could tell us whether you had any contacts with Mr. Rodic and to tell us very briefly what information he sought from you and what information you provided to him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Rodic personally. We only spoke on the phone once, twice at the most. As he was drafting his expert report, he wanted to know with greater specificity what equipment we used at one or two locations in order to be able to provide a credible expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your proofing for the evidence here, when the two of us met, could you please tell me whether you had an opportunity to acquaint yourself with his expert report, to read it, to look at it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell me in general terms, I don't want to go into any details, but can you tell me whether this expert report reflects faithfully the organisation and the functioning of the communications in the Drina Corps while you were the commander of the 5th Signals Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have already said that I don't want to go into details, but let me just deal with some issues. First of all, could you please tell me whether there was a radio relay communication, a direct radio relay axis between Vlasenica and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly why it was that this radio relay axis was not set up, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been very happy had there been such a possibility, because it would have made our communications system more flexible, but simply the nature of the dispersion of the electro-magnetic waves at frequencies used by this type of equipment is such that they require a line of vision. There has to be a line of vision. The two spots, the two aerials, have to be eye-to-eye, and it was impossible to do that between Vlasenica and Zvornik because there are several geographical obstacles that disrupt the line of vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me briefly how the communication line was established between Vlasenica and Zvornik since there was no direct line?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to establish communications with Zvornik, because of the geographical situation, the lay of the land, we had to use three radio relay nodes in order to reach Zvornik indirectly. The communications were set up using four radio relay sections. The first radio relay section was Vlasenica-Veliki Zep. The second one was Veliki Zep-Cer. The third one was Cer-Gucevo. And the fourth one was Cer-Zvornik -- or, rather, Gucevo-Zvornik, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell me, at those sections, what equipment was used? Was it one equipment, one device, several devices, and what kinds?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of these sections was covered by two radio relay devices. So the entire line, radio relay line, was covered by eight devices. At the first, third, and fourth sections we used radio relay devices RRU800. And in the second section, between stationary node Veliki Zep and the Cer stationary node, we used a radio relay device with a larger channel capacity called MSC [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said SMC?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you this. We have this organisational chart. I don't think that we need to look at it anymore. We saw that between Veliki Zep and Cer there was another direction or axis where it is indicated that an RRU80 [as interpreted] device was used, and could you tell us whether this axis functioned or whether it didn't function, what was its role, what was it used for?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a backup axis because this radio relay section was very important for us. It carried a large number of channels used by a variety of users, not only in the military but also political figures. And that is why a plan was made to have this backup axis. If the first radio relay axis is disrupted, we usually -- when we did our charts, we drew those backup lines with broken lines. I don't have it now in front of me, but this is how we usually drew in the backup axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have in the translation "RRU80." Is that right or is that a new machine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you can clarify that. It's line 24 of the previous page, at least on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your answer is interpreted as saying "RRU80." So could you please repeat what kind of radio relay device was used.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: RRU800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you this: To the best of your knowledge and recollection, we are interested in July 1995, do you recall whether the radio relay, the backup line or the backup axis, actually functioned between Veliki Zep and Cer or was it actually only the SMC that was actually functioning?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no knowledge of the radio relay axis using the SMC being disrupted which would require the activation of the backup line using RRU800 devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you another document from this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's 1D322. That's the annex to the report. Pages 13 and 14 in the English version. However, this document is in the B/C/S, so I would like us to look at P2823. It's a Prosecution exhibit because it does have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think you remember this, but please tell me if you do. These are the frequencies used by RRU800 device, and now I would like to ask you first: Do you recall having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document in the course of the proofing sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you now tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down a little bit, both of you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me now, there are some frequencies used by the RRU800 device. As the commander of the 5th Signals Battalion, were you able to switch frequencies?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could this be done by anyone from your unit, let's say, people operating those devices?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could it have been done by, let's say, your signals chief in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even the signals chief in the Drina Corps was authorised to make those changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell me regarding this document, to the best of your recollection -- I know that you see that this document dates from 1993. So to the best of your recollection, were these frequencies changed in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so because there was no need to change them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I would like to show you a document, it's a Prosecution Exhibit 1468. It's a map that the BH army had indicating the disposition of the radio relay communications devices of the army of Republika Srpska. This is the work map of the counter-electronic warfare section of the 2nd Krajina Corps, and as you can see, it refers to the period between January and September 1995. Could you please tell us, did you have an opportunity in the course of the proofing sessions for your evidence here to see this map?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you to tell me whether this map reflects the situation as it existed in the communications system of the Drina Corps. I will now limit myself only to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.
