utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us in what way does it not reflect the situation. At least in the roughest terms, what is it that is not an accurate reflection of the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could just ask the usher to show the lower, the bottom part of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would it help the witness more if we gave him the original document? Otherwise, we will -- I will have to zoom in because the names, the topological names are barely visible. Do you have it available?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can go get it, Mr. President. This is first time I've heard of any of this. I don't have a proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's -- Mr. Jevdjevic, and Mr. Zivanovic, are you interested in the point where all these lines converge towards the bottom of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's zoom there for the time being. And see whether we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I am trying to help. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can perhaps look at the hard copy and then you will be able to give us a more accurate description. I will not be asking you to make any markings.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me start by explaining and indicating the differences between the actual situation, the way in which our radio relay communications were set up, and what is in line with the radio relay chart that I saw in the documents at the relevant time-period. First of all, this radio relay node of Veliki Zep is where all the lines go out. It's like a centre of a circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case perhaps you can just mark it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this here is the stationary node Veliki Zep and this is indeed true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with 1.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was the key radio relay node for the organisation of the radio relay communications of the Main Staff and the Drina Corps whose radio relay line to Vlasenica was just some 15 kilometres away. First of all, this radio relay line or direction, this one here, did not exist. And this intelligence organ and the counter-electronic warfare organ from the 2nd Corps indicated this direction as leading from Veliki Zep to Gucevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could I now ask you to mark this with number 2.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Furthermore, this -- the second radio relay line, if we go from the direction of north and then clockwise, this one here, indicated as leading from Veliki Zep to Milici, the Milici Brigade, did not exist. I will mark it as 3 because as far as the Milici Brigade was concerned, in the 13 kilometres between Vlasenica and Milici we had a landline, and it was impossible to set it up because of the line of vision problems and it was unnecessary because there was a landline which was almost completely surveillance proof. The third radio relay line, Gric-Vrelo, I don't know what unit it refers to, but in that area which is marked here, we only had -- we may have had an engineer regiment in Konjevic Polje. I can see that this line extends to them, but we did not have a radio relay line with them, because from Kasaba on we had a landline. I personally laid it. So that did not exist either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with 4 to prevent any confusion because you marked it with three.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The so-called thick line, the fourth line, that's what we called it, the thick line, because it had a multitude of channels, that is correct. It used the SMC device, and I'll mark it with 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be good for you to limit yourself to the details that did not reflect the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. So with Skelani we did not have a direct radio relay line. We used land-lines going through the territory of Serbia so that this line here is not correct. I'll mark it with 6. Then this line that is indicated here, where it says "The Rogatica Brigade," is not correct because we used the stationary node Strazbenice in Montenegro with them because there was no line of sight. This thick line for Veliki Tmor, well, Veliki Tmor is a TV tour. There is a TV tower there but the military never used the communications, not before the war, not during the war, because this was rugged train, impassable. And I will mark it with 8. This line here for Pale, Pale also had the communications line from Strazbenice to Jahorina and then onwards so that there was no thick line Zepa-Pale. This line with the Sokolac Brigade, where it says "The breach," did not exist. I will mark it with 10, because the radio relay line with the Sokolac Brigade was carried out through radio relay lines Veliki Zep-Strazbenice, Strazbenice-Sokolac. So we did not have a direct line because, simply, there was no line of sight from Sokolac to Veliki Zep. Here where it says "The 2nd Romanija Brigade." This line did not exist either. I will mark it with 11, because the command at Knezina was connected with the landline. 12 channels operated in Knezina. There was an aerial line, in fact, that was used primarily for civilian purposes. And then this line to Zlatar, here at Vlasenica, it is marked here but it is marked at the Visalac [phoen] feature and that's wrong; it's not here. It's in the town itself. Where the arrow is marking the command, that's where the station was located. So here this is where the command was. We had it on the command building. This is very important for the radio relay communications, because they go from one point to another. So this line did not exist the way it is drawn here. So this document should have been drafted on the basis of the intelligence data that the 2nd Corps of the BH army had. And on the basis of all that, they were supposed to give instructions to their units, the electronic reconnaissance units and their audio surveillance stations, to direct their receivers, their aerials, in order to optimise reception. And this is my opinion, but everybody can compare it with our chart for the radio relay communications for the relevant period. So all the changes that I drew in, everybody can mark them. Everybody can see that they are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would just like to ask you this. Do you notice -- do you think that the features used by the Main Staff are marked correctly here? Can you -- or the facilities used by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff is marked as being in Han Pijesak, and in fact, it was located just below Veliki Zep in the facilities in an area called Crna Rijeka. And I think that's some 11 kilometres away from Han Pijesak itself, from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this facility marked with an aerial is actually wrongly marked?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, this line. It --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we are missing something. You have been overlapping, and as a result the interpreters couldn't catch up. Could the interpreters help me exactly where they found difficulties. The last that we have is Mr. Zivanovic's question saying: "Does that mean that this facility marked with an aerial is actually wrongly marked?" And we then had -- I think you can start from there, Mr. Jevdjevic. Could you start your answer -- your reply again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's wrongly marked, because the Main Staff or, rather, the command post of the Main Staff was located at Crna Rijeka and there was no relay up to that location. Instead, there was a wire line, a cable, from Crna Rijeka to the Veliki Zep node so that this relay axis here did not exist for the needs of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very nice, but we are not receiving interpretation. Now it's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you have already replied to the question; but in any case, if you think you haven't, tell us. What were the practical consequences if, on a map like this, the true axes and the true facilities through which listening in to enemy conversations were carried out are not entered correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This working map and its reliability is very important because it is on this basis that information is provided to the units for electronic reconnaissance. That is, in what direction they should point their aerials so as to best listen in to the conversations of the enemy side. If it's approximate, just an approximate sketch like this one of our radio relay connections and command posts, I ask myself how it's possible to organise precise listening in to these communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, I'll ask you a question about your going to Zepa in the evening of the 11th and your arrival on the 12th. I would like to know when you arrived -- or, rather, when you arrived did you see any soldiers there, any smaller units? Was anyone still there or did anyone arrive after you arrived, right after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at the Pribicevac [as interpreted] forward command post on the 12th, first I found a small unit there, a platoon from the protection regiment, the 65th Protection Regiment, which was holding defence positions and controlling the territory. At the entrance to the village of Pod Plane, a unit had already arrived from Visegrad which was to join in the Stupcanica 95 operation later. They had arrived directly from Visegrad. They had not been at Srebrenica, and with their communications man, I exchanged the indispensable information. And I saw some small groups of soldiers, I don't know whether they were logistics men or people reconnoitering the locations where these other units were supposed to arrive, but I don't really remember them. They didn't seem significant to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think there must be a mistake in line 15. I don't think that the witness said that he arrived in Pribicevac on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jevdjevic. Here at the beginning of your last answer to Mr. Zivanovic's question, we have in the transcript: "When I arrived at the Pribicevac forward ..." That is obviously a mistake. On the 12th, command post on the 12th. Where did you arrive on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Krivace forward command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, I would like to ask you to sign this map and put today's date on it. Today is the 12th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can this be saved, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jevdjevic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, my name is John Ostojic and I represent Ljubisa Beara. Good afternoon to you, sir. I have a couple of questions for you, and bear with me, and I apologise if they seem repetitive, but I just want to have a better understanding of these intercepts and some of the work that you do. First of all, before we get into the intercepts, can you tell me who -- or whether or not your commander was a gentleman by the name of Eric?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of my immediate subordinates, there was no one called Eric. There may have been someone in the 2nd Romanija Brigade, a lower ranking commander of that last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 2nd Romanija Brigade, I think there was a reserve captain called Ljubo Eric, if he is the one you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it is actually Ljubo Eric. Can you tell me, sir, moving along, who was your direct superior in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My direct superior at the forward command post in July was General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First, how many subordinates did you have in July of 1995, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of the Communications Battalion, and it was the company commanders in that communications battalion who were my subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what are their names?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time one of them was Captain Zeljko Drljaca, and I think the other one was Captain Ranko Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me switch gears a little bit. Are you familiar with the 5th Podrinje Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who led that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was Lieutenant-Colonel Furtula.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just focusing on specifically July of 1995, was the 5th Podrinje Infantry Brigade involved in any of the activity or actions with respect to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there may have been a platoon from that brigade engaged in one of those subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of that platoon?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure exactly what the name of the platoon was, but more or less, the information I have, although we didn't talk about this, was that there was a platoon from that brigade in Operation Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now turning to the Zepa action, were they involved, the 5th Podrinje Infantry Brigade, in the Zepa operation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From what date to what date?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived in their holding area on the 12th, when I was there, and remained there until the end of Stupcanica 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Commander Furtula there from the 12th through the, let's say, the 2nd of August, 1995? And when we say "there," I think we are talking about specifically the Krivace area, where you were at one of the forward command posts. And I recognise there were three and we will get into that a little later, but ...

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who was his superior at that time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, taking -- focussing you on the period back now to the 5th through the 11th of July, 1995, when you were at the forward command post -- we've identified it as Pribicevac, can you tell me, sir, at that time - and I know we looked at a couple of exhibits - whether or not General Krstic was there during that entire time-period, the 5th through the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there throughout this period; and in the evening, I think he would go to Bratunac to spend the night there, because it was required for his health.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, sir, in understanding your testimony that in the evening of the 11th of July, 1995, you left with your communications centre from Pribicevac and you went to Bratunac, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you spent the night, generally, on the 11th of July, 1995, in the area of Bratunac and then you were ordered to proceed to or towards Zepa and to establish a forward command post, as we've identified it, being Krivace, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't spend the night there, but I was there during that part of the night when that order arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. It was my understanding that you went to Krivace on the 12th of July at approximately 1400 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But in the night of the 11th, at about 11.00 in the evening, I left Bratunac and arrived at the command post of the corps in Vlasenica, and I spent the night in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, I have a curious question. You mentioned in your prior testimony that you set up three forward command posts in Zepa, and I apologise if I'm going to mispronounce them. One is obviously Krivace. The other one is Godjenje, and the third one is Zlovrh; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlovrh, yes. Those were three forward command posts because that's how the combat disposition changed and the forward command post followed the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you, you're anticipating my question. Just reflecting back on the Zepa action -- I mean the Srebrenica action, it only had one forward command post during that entire time from the 5th to the 11th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now let's talk a little bit about the intercepts and to maybe draw from some of your experience that you have, and I'm grateful to discuss it with you. I've seen that from the intercepts that there are several key elements that we need to look at; in essence, maybe seven, from what I can discern. And one would be that we would identify the azimuth, the frequency, the channel, the direction, the participants if possible, and obviously the date and the time. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are there any other elements that are necessary in order to have a complete and thorough reflection of an intercept that is purportedly captured, other than those seven elements that we've just described?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Looking, generally speaking, at the intercepts, and we've seen some that my learned friend Mr. Haynes had shown you, are we able to determine where a participant or where the participants were at a given time and date, if we know simply the channel, for example? Or is it necessary to have all of the seven factors in order to conclude with specificity where the participants may have been?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of most of these intercepts, one would need to take into account quite a few elements in order to be able to say with precision where the participants were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at P1171, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's an exhibit that you looked at during your direct examination. And just so I can get a better understanding of it, do you see the frequency there of being 285.850? Oh, 255, I'm sorry, point 850. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you, just looking at the frequency, tell us where the call was either made from or coming to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we had an RRU1 radio relay piece of equipment between the forward command post and Veliki Zep. I assume this was the 15th of July, and this frequency tells us that this was an RRU1. At that time we had relay communications with these pieces of equipment organised on the Krivace-Veliki Zep line. So if all this has been taken down correctly and if the conversation has been properly intercepted, one of the participants was at Krivace, the forward command post at Krivace. As for the other participant, it's hard to establish where he was because after Veliki Zep he could have called from a location unknown to me and a distance unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I am not sure I understand. How is it that it cannot be known to you? I mean, you're a communications guy. With just having one frequency, are we able to discern where both participants in a given conversation are with only one frequency that's identified? Or is it because many possibilities exist?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on the basis of the frequency one cannot know from where the participants spoke. I assume that this conversation was intercepted somewhere between Krivace and Veliki Zep. As Krivace is the ultimate, the final relay station, someone had to speak from there, and I assume one of the participants was at Krivace for that reason. Then, the similar transits from Veliki Zep towards Vlasenica and from Vlasenica to the entire area of responsibility of the corps, and one cannot know for certain from which location this other participant answered the call because the intercept was intercepted between Veliki Zep and Krivace. And there are many possibilities beyond that. We enter into a whole network of communications, and one participant could come in from any number of directions. I hope you understand me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do. Thank you for that. Now, let me try to see if I could -- or you could help me decode some of this. Just looking at this, 255.850, is it fair to say that every time we see this frequency, that indicates that it came from Krivace or went to the Krivace-Veliki Zep area, at least that part of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we had organised communications with RRU1 on some other directions of secondary importance. But this text, I think, deals with the Krivace forward command post and that's why I think that that was part of that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what about other numbers or other frequencies. If I give you a couple, maybe you could help me understand them. Like, where would 254.300 -- where would that frequency be located, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another frequency from the range of the RRU1 equipment. So as the conversation was intercepted where two participants were communicating using that radio relay section.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But where would it be, where specifically would it be geographically?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Geographically? Well, there was a direction between Krivace and Veliki Zep, so I assume one of the participants was at Krivace and the other -- it's hard to say where he was. You saw that network represented schematically. They all come to Veliki Zep, and then from Veliki Zep there is a line going to Krivace. I cannot say now where that signal went or, rather, where this participant came from to Veliki Zep in order to enter the section from Veliki Zep to Krivace.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm just waiting for the translation. Thank you, sir. I am just trying to have a better -- maybe a layperson's understanding. When the forward command post, whether it was at Pribicevac or Krivace, if they were to be connected with, let's hypothetically say, the Bratunac Brigade, can someone calling from an area outside of Bratunac, whether it's within the Republika Srpska or even Serbia, can they be connected through Bratunac to the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you just explain that for me. If someone was calling outside, let's even take Zvornik because it's there, if someone was calling from the Zvornik zone, if they called Bratunac and asked for someone, can Bratunac connect them to a forward command post like Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Would there be any indication on the actual intercept that that call came through Bratunac from another part of the country in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let me concretely ask you this. I mentioned a little bit Serbia, how about if someone was in Belgrade and they called Bratunac and asked to be connected to the forward command post. Can they be -- is that probable or possible?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible, absolutely. In all the communications centres of the brigades we had telephone switch boards, and these switchboards were used to connect various kinds of participants. And there was a post office number, a Telekom number, such as all the inhabitants of Bratunac had. And then, on another place of the -- in the same switchboard we had the corps command in Bratunac and some battalions in that brigade. So it would be sufficient for someone from Belgrade or anywhere else in the world to dial that Telekom number which ended up at the switchboard in the Bratunac Brigade and to ask for the corps command in Vlasenica or simply to ask for Pribicevac. The communications man would know how to connect him up to Pribicevac, because that's what the switchboard was used for, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I asked you a little bit about the 200 series frequency, namely 255 and 254. Can you tell me about the 700 series, and I am talking about after July -- or approximately July 15, 1995, when you were at Krivace; for example, 784.650. If you could help me, do you remember what that frequency was, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a frequency from the range of the RRU800 radio relay device.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me what the range is specifically, sir. How far does it go above or below the frequency that I just identified 784.650? Is it up or down a hundred or up or down more than that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the frequency range of that device, which is from 610 to 960 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And similarly with respect to the RRU1, what was the range of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's significantly different. There is also a significant difference in the characteristics of those electro-magnetic waves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just quickly ask you to help me look at Exhibit P3753, which I think is a communication plan for Srebrenica or -- that you discussed. 3753.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if we could just enlarge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, we looked at a couple of these columns during your examination here, and we do note that there are specifically 22 different areas here on the middle or towards the left-hand section, but just help me understand this a little bit. After the number one, two -- three, you see the different designations for the frequency. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now just help me to understand that. Is that the frequency that those specific brigades or platoons or units were given that frequency at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We started work at the first frequency. In fact, it's not the frequency, it's the channel designation. So this device has three switches, A, B, C, where you jump from one frequency to another. And it was much easier for us to write 250, that's a channel, one of the channels which corresponds to a certain frequency. And at the beginning and end of this operation, we worked only on that channel, on that frequency. The other frequencies, up until number 22 [Realtime transcript read in error "222"], whoever drafted this plan merely envisaged them as a possibility. If something should go wrong, in terms of security of the communications, if our encryption devices fail to function properly, then this was planned so that we could switch from channel to channel lest the enemy should catch us out on just one frequency. But this did not occur, and there was no need for us to use the backup frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do have a few more minutes, like, 15 possibly. So I don't know if it's time for a break or I can proceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies to the interpreters. If you have 15 minutes, I think we better have the break now. Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a few questions for you to just follow-up on a couple of issues. We did talk about the 2nd Romanija Brigade, and in looking -- and you still have this exhibit in front of you, 3753, is it listed here as being part -- I think on the fourth row, is that part of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just so that I am clear, the person or the commander of that brigade is Ljubo Eric, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of that brigade was Colonel Trivic, and commander of his battalion, the battalion that took part in the attack -- in Krivaja 95, rather, was Captain First Class Ljubo Eric. He was later promoted to major. I don't know whether he was major at that time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because it may be considered a common name, but do you know what his full name is? Do you know if he goes by -- is it Ljubo or does he have another full name like Ljubisa or Ljubislav or Ljubomir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that his full name was Ljubomir, but we all called him Ljubo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now a couple of other questions if I can - thank you for this exhibit - go back to the frequencies and the RRU1 and the RRU800 that you described. And I know -- and I apologise and you can correct me if I'm wrong, you talked about the ranges for both frequencies, is it possible or to the best of your knowledge can a conversation be intercepted from both an RRU1 and an RRU800 machine simultaneously, meaning the same conversation? Or is that impossible?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible to intercept a conversation at a section, but you have to have two surveillance groups. One listening in on the section where the RRU1 is operating at a certain frequency; and the other surveillance group needs to eavesdrop on a completely different relay line in a different geographical area where RRU800 devices are used. That is the only way in which it is possible to audio surveil a single conversation at different sections, but you need to have several surveillance groups to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I think that's all I have. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, one, I'm sorry, Mr. President. And I'm sorry, my learned friend. There was an error on the transcript before the break at page 63, line 11 -- 14. And I think the witness said "222" -- it should be recorded as "22" but it's reflected as "222." If we could just note that and double-check that, we'd appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He said: "The other frequencies up until number 22."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And I think we could see it on the exhibit itself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Although we have had the opportunity of meeting earlier this week, for the record, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon and today I am accompanied with my colleague Dragan Djukic, and together we represent Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. I have a few questions to ask you in respect of five specific areas, and I will do my best to complete today before 1345. The first area I would like to get into, I would like to clarify a few points regarding the establishment of communications and, of course, the possibility for the enemy to intercept such communications. So, of course, it's a common theme this morning, but I will try to make my questions quite precise in order to clarify this area. First, I would like to get a confirmation from you that documents could be sent by teleprinter between the Drina Corps command and the Main Staff, as well as between the Drina Corps command and subordinate brigades of the Drina Corps by secure means; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when we say "secure means" for sending documents, or when we say that a document is encrypted, can you confirm that the encryption of a document does not require the use of any codes, that encryption is a mechanical purpose; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to oral communications or oral conversations between the Drina Corps command and the Main Staff, and I insist here my question is precisely with the Main Staff. Can you confirm that both ways of transmission were available: A secure line with a limited possibility and the other line which you have described, the open line, working partly with wire communications - that is the telephone or the handset - going through the radio relay; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. You said at the beginning that radio communications were -- you had mentioned radio communications and we are talking about radio relay communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you for this correction. Now, I've mentioned -- of course, I am talking specifically now here with oral conversations between the Drina Corps command and the Main Staff, but I guess you would agree that this -- the same applies for the Drina Corps IKM or forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I look at oral conversations between the Drina Corps command or the Drina Corps IKM with its subordinate brigades, the same thing applies; that is, we have an open line going through radio relay but there was no secure means for oral conversations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not have the encryption device for the radio relay lines from the corps to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you've answered previously during your examination-in-chief, a conversation between someone calling from the Bratunac area, for example, calling the Zvornik Brigade or the Zvornik Brigade IKM, for that matter, this is a conversation that could be intercepted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it goes through radio relay devices that did not have the protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, a number of intercepts have been shown to you since the beginning of your testimony, and I take it that you are also able to confirm, based on your experience, that conversations going through radio relay, no codes were used for such conversations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversations were mostly done over open line without speech protection, but the usual practice among the officers was to speak in the usual way, but to -- when mentioning important information, to do it in such a way that it is not comprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But there was no use of codes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And "no" meaning no codes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I move on to communications using military inductor phones, I take it you know when I mean when I say military inductor phones?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that this is a secure means of communications, that conversations cannot be intercepted when you have wire between two military inductor phones?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a fairly secure -- almost 100 per cent secure. There can be no eavesdropping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And of course using those military inductor phones, which were linked by wire, the practice was not to use codes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I move on to radio communications, not radio relay but specifically radio communications, and if I refer to Krivaja 95 -- first that during this operation you testified already that you were using a radio that looked or that was almost the same as a RUP-12 with the specificity that you added a scrambling device; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my colleague asked you a question of you yesterday and you confirm that it was your belief, and you haven't seen any evidence to the contrary, that all radio communications during Krivaja 95 using this scrambling device, that those communications were secure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not have any knowledge, and I don't have any knowledge now, that those lines -- that it was possible to surveil those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on this basis -- and of course considering that you were on the ground at the time and you did listen to this radio network, you can confirm that no codes were used when using the radio with the scrambling device?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I move on to radio communications using the RUP-12 without the scrambling device, you will agree with me that this, of course, is a not secure means of communications that can be easily intercepted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is where the codes that we find in your communications plan, that's where they could become useful; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But I take it you will also agree with me that the use of codes is a very time-consuming process; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you in a position to confirm that, in fact, very few members of the VRS were trained in -- to using codes, whether to code or decode information on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depending on the unit. The practice and the level of discipline that the unit imposed on its lower levels, battalions, and companies, I cannot generalise now; but I do know that major messages were encoded using the slow method, and I know that there was quite a lot of open communication going on, which made it possible for important information to leak out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the best way, in fact, if you don't want to use codes using the RUP-12, that the best way to protect information is to change frequency regularly and, even more importantly, to keep the communications as short as possible?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is one of the ways in which it is possible to protect a line from being surveilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you go as far as confirming that discipline imposed when using RUP-12 would be to, indeed, keep the conversations to very, very, short transmissions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a rule that we applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, there is one more means of communication I would like to cover with you and that is to send documents by courier. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, courier is the most -- is the securest form of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you for this answer. I was going to quote you from your testimony in the Krstic case, where you referred in fact, and I quote here from transcript 7178, to the rule that "the safest communications is by courier." Now, in the same case -- in the Krstic case when you testified, you said that: "There was no use of courier from the Drina Corps forward command post at Pribicevac, as it was not practical due to the distance." Do you confirm that today?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of Operation Krivaja 95, to the best of my recollection, couriers were not used because relied on the radio communications that we used. We relied on them being secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also said in the same case at 7178, and you were talking at that moment specifically for the forward command post in Krivace, that the distances were closer. You mention six kilometres between the forward command post and the Main Staff Command, and 30-odd kilometres between the forward command post and the Drina Corps command. Are these distances more or less correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also stated in that case that although you did not plan to use couriers, it is quite possible that written messages were sent by drivers. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at it logically because it was only six kilometres from the Main Staff while we were at Krivace. And the time it took for the cryptographer to type out the information on the teleprinter, to set up the line and to send it, it was faster to just drive there by car, but I don't recall any specific actions of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question with respect to couriers. A military expert testified in this case, and I refer to the transcript at 26269, and he was asked to comment on the use of couriers. And his answer was the following, I quote from lines 20 to 23: "That is why one sends a courier to deal with anything confidential and to make sure that none of the elements of information are caught and that the information be delivered with precision." Would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when those two operations were carried out, I don't recall -- or, rather, I don't know that I organised and I didn't notice that anyone else organised couriers running towards the Main Staff or the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my question was not precise enough, but the statement that I just read to you from this military expert, do you agree that sending a courier is a very good way to deal with confidential information and to ensure that the information, of course, is not intercepted but also that the information is delivered with precision? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to my second area, dealing with some questions that were put to you concerning the 10th Sabotage Detachment. First, you stated yesterday and you can confirm that this unit appeared on 10 July 1995 in the area of Pribicevac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the Krstic case when you testified, you said the following, that is T7086: "I think they arrived in the area only a day or two before Srebrenica fell militarily, which means a day or two prior to the 11th." On this basis, my question is: I take it that they could have, in fact, arrived on the 9th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a comparison and it stuck in my mind that they reached that area approximately the same day when General Mladic did, perhaps give or take one or two days in this period. Having analysed those activities -- so I really still claim that it was a day or two, the 10th or the 9th, but now it seems to me that it may have been the 10th for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you for that precision. Now, can you confirm that when this unit appeared in the area of Pribicevac, that of course the VRS had not yet entered into Srebrenica, that we know, but I would like you to confirm that on that day the Drina Corps possessed very little, if any, information regarding the intentions of the 28th Division to move towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have the information, accurate information, about the actual intentions of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you also stated that this unit, that what you -- what your interest in this unit was, is that you wanted to know when you would be required to provide them -- to provide them, sorry, with the scrambling device; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you stated yesterday, that was at page 67, lines 9 to 12, that in an effort to find a solution, you asked General Krstic, and I quote from the transcript, asking him: "When I would be asked to provide them with such equipment and what activities they would be involved in order to be able to exercise command over them." My question is the following: What was General Krstic's answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall the exact answer, but generally my memory is that it was introduced between Pribicevac and Kvarac, between the two hills along a valley, connecting the forces that were attacking in the direction of Srebrenica. They were part of those forces. And since this was a unit of 20 to 30 -- 20 to 30 soldiers strong, I did not think that they could make any contribution, significant contribution, in military terms. But I assume that they had some kind of a special mission within the purview of what they were doing, their special purpose, whether it was removing mines or perhaps preparing for street fighting, fighting in a built-up area, which was something that they were equipped for. I came across a piece of information earlier that they had tried to enter an area in the enclave using the mining tunnels that were leading in that direction, so I assume that they had a special mission in combat terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And of course you assume, but you did not have this information. Other than this last piece of information, you did not know exactly what they were doing there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General Krstic, of course, was aware of the arrival of this unit in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you had this conversation with the signal man from the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and he told you that they had Motorolas, that this was sufficient for them, and that he had no intention to carry a large piece of equipment around with him. That was at 29587, lines 7 to 9. And my question is: The reason why he did not want your scrambling device was because they had the communications they needed and he did not want to carry a heavy radio with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at 29587, you said that this signal man told you that they had some special assignment. Now, he did not say to you "secret assignment," did he?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I asked this question because I -- when we met, in some proofing notes that I saw the word "secret" was there, but you informed me and you can confirm that this was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had some kind of a special mission. That's the way I understood it and that's the way I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the same thing eight years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you also mention, and I'd like to confirm, that the reason or one of the reasons you did not pay attention to this conversation with the signal man from the 10th Sabotage Detachment was that both General Krstic and General Mladic were there, so they must have known what was going on with that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to my next area of questioning, and I'd like to show a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can I have in e-court please 4D124.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And while we wait for this document that will appear before you, I would just like to confirm what you said in your testimony in the Krstic case, that you read this document when preparing for your testimony in that case. That's at 7104, lines 18 to 22. So did you read this document when preparing for your testimony in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said so then, I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, do you recall that today? I am not wanting to ...

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read this document now, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember reviewing this document when preparing for your testimony in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not deny anything I said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. It's not -- there is no trap. It's just simply to confirm, because I am not sure if we referred yet to your interview with the Prosecution, but you can confirm that you were interviewed by the Prosecution in April of 2000. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at page 7150 of this interview, you stated the following, and I quote: "During preparations for this interview, I was told that it took place on the 13th." "It" being the issuance of this document. "At the time, I knew it happened but I cannot recall the exact date, but I know it actually happened at the beginning of the attack on Zepa." My question today is: On this basis, can you confirm that this actually happened at the beginning of the attack on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we clarify what "this" means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: "This" being that this document and the change of command over the Drina Corps from General Zivanovic to General Krstic happened on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is the first time this document appeared before the Chamber -- or, rather, it appeared on the 19th of April, 2001, for the first time. The witness was interviewed on the 4th of April, 2000, by the OTP and testified in the Krstic case in November 2000. So that this document was not available at the time of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My memory is the same as Mr. Petrusic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I mean, the Prosecution can take this up on -- in his -- in his cross-examination if he wants, but the transcript I have from Krstic, at 7104, the witness said that he saw the document when he was preparing for his testimony in that case. That's where I get my information and that was the basis for my questions. So it's no big deal, and I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, this is a very big deal. It was a very big deal. Mr. Petrusic and I remember it as such, so I think we had better check on that before we deal with this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will move on and if I am not finished I can clarify this on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to suggest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, what I would like you to confirm -- it's my last question and I am not sure if you did answer this, and the question was: That the change of command between General Zivanovic and General Krstic, that, as you said in your interview, you knew that it actually happened at the beginning of the attack on Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that a change of corps commander is a major happening?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that in military terms and in logical terms it is very important when there is a change of command that everyone be informed as quickly as possible?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, logically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we go back to this document, which is 4D124, I draw your attention to the last line of the document, just above the signature block, where it says: "Acquaint all members of your unit in appropriate manner with this document." So my question is the following: As we can see from this document, it was received by the Zvornik Brigade, and we can also see that it was transmitted on the 13th and received on the 14th at some point. Can you confirm that upon receiving such a document, everyone would be informed of this change, and especially the commander of the unit, if he's there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was at the Krivace forward command post, I, myself, so that this document did not arrive at the forward command post, and this information as to the hand-over of duty is not something I was clear about because my information was only secondhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But as a matter of principle, you can confirm that when the Zvornik Brigade received that document, that it would disseminate the information because it is important to know when there is a change of a corps commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. It's quite logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the sake of saving some time, I have two documents I would like to show you. Maybe we can cut short, and I'll just ask you this question: If I have two documents, the first one being signed by General Zivanovic as commander at 1610 hours, I refer here to 7DP1032, on the 13th of July, and I have a second document signed by General Krstic as commander at or about 1945 hours on the 13th of July, is that a reliable indicator that the change of command has indeed taken place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you going to show that document or are you just asking me the question without showing the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, if you want I can show you those documents, but the just -- one is signed by Zivanovic at 4.00 and one is signed by Krstic at 1945. Is that a good indicator that the change of command has taken place? And I think the Prosecution will take up on that later, so I just want to know from you whether you believe, on the basis of your experience, that this is a good indicator?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the document that arrived later was signed by General Krstic using the title "Corps Commander" without the "for" in front, then that would imply that he was the corps commander at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think that might be covered by others in cross-examination. I move on to -- I only have two more areas. My colleague asked you some questions about a telephone conversation you had with Major Obrenovic, and you said this conversation took place at some point on the 14th of July, 1995. Do you recall what conversation I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On what means did you receive this phone call?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An automatic telephone, a normal telephone, attached to the RRU1 device.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that would mean that this conversation between wherever Major Obrenovic was at the time and you, went through radio relay; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that Major Obrenovic could not have used a radio RUP-12 for this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct. He had to call me from a place where he also had a telephone, whether an induction telephone or one with a dial; but in any case, he could only have called me and communicated with me using a telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I only have two more questions, and I think we can finish today. In the Krstic case when you testified, a question was put to you by Judge Wald concerning intercepts. This is on page 7114 and 7115. Her question was the following: "If there were mistakes or if an intercept did not accurately reflect what had actually been said between the parties, where is it most likely the mistake would have been made, on the side of the monitoring person who was listening who did not understand or, I mean, where is it most likely that the thing went wrong if, in fact, at the end of the intercept didn't reflect what actually went on in the conversation? Where is the most likely area that it would have broken down?" That was the Judge -- the question put to you by the Judge. Your answer was: "Based on my experience, most probably where it would have broken down would be the individual monitoring the conversation, because as a rule, those conversations are taped and then they are transcribed and recorded on the basis of what is listened to and heard." And at the end you say: "According to our regulations, those individuals would have had to spend five years doing that kind of work to be considered competent to sift through the correct information from the incorrect and the important and unimportant." Do you stand by your answer and can you add to this today?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My last question is the following. Also in your testimony in the Krstic case, you were asked about the command and the officers and their experience in 1995. And you stated at 7132: "I also wish to note that this was the year 1995 when the command and officer cadres already had a great deal of experience and only a few input information was required by all the assistants for them to be able to act more speedily than the theory envisages the procedure to take and which I have tried to describe to you." And that had to do with the drafting of orders. My question is the following: Do you agree that by 1995 the level of experience within the VRS in general was much better than at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I might come back on Monday morning, Mr. President, just to clarify this one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you very much, sir.
